frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d174: Roosevelt wrote to Secretary Hull on October 30, 1943, in a letter placed in the Moscow section as Document 174 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d274:
A memorandum of conversation dated 26 November 1943, kept secret, records John Winant and an unnamed American colleague talking with British foreign secretary Anthony Eden about the European Advisory Commission. The body, set up at the Moscow conference, was meant to handle questions arising as the war in Europe ended.

The Americans worry that too much post-hostility planning has been handed to a London body at the start, which could stall real work and sour American opinion. Eden pushes back, calling the commission an achievement backed by Secretary Hull, and warns against seeming to slight it before the Soviets. The meeting settles on a working path: commission proposals would pass through the Combined Chiefs of Staff for comment before going to the governments.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d374:
Minutes kept for the Combined Chiefs of Staff record the same plenary session at Tehran on 30 November 1943 at four in the afternoon, in the staff version paralleling the Bohlen minutes. The decisions and pledges are the same, set down for the military record.

Brooke reads the staff conclusions: Overlord in May 1944, plus a supporting operation against the south of France at the largest scale the landing craft of the time permit. Churchill promises to keep Stalin and the Soviet staff informed as the circle closes on Germany, and hopes Yugoslav resistance and a Turkish entry will add pressure. Stalin repeats his undertaking to mount a large-scale offensive in May to contain the most German divisions possible in the east. Roosevelt closes the military business by promising the supreme commander's appointment within days of reaching Cairo.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d474:
Two days after the Tehran Conference ended, on December 3, 1943, President Roosevelt wrote to Marshal Stalin. The two leaders had met face to face for the first time at Tehran, where they agreed on the broad course of the war. The State Department printed this follow-up message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Roosevelt treated his direct line to Stalin as a key tool of the alliance, and the days right after Tehran were full of loose ends to tie off. A message from this moment shows the President working to keep the new personal relationship warm. It forms part of the famous Roosevelt-Stalin correspondence that ran through the war.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d574:
The Secretary of State wrote to the President on September 3, 1945. That was the day after Japan's formal surrender. The surrender took place aboard the Missouri. James F. Byrnes then led the department under President Truman. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

A secretary's letter on the first day of peace belongs to a great transition. Armies had to be brought home. Settlements had to be negotiated. Pledges made at Tehran and Cairo had to be honored or revised. For readers, the message closes the volume's war story. It also opens the aftermath. The department was turning from coalition warfare to a divided peace.
frus-1944-quebec-d74:
Assistant Secretary of War John J. McCloy wrote on August 28, 1944. His recipient was H. Freeman Matthews, a senior European affairs official. The State Department printed the letter in its Quebec 1944 volume. McCloy often linked the War Department with the diplomats.

War and State officials had to align their views on Europe. The Quebec Conference opened two weeks later in Canada. Leaders there faced the treatment of a defeated Germany. For readers, the letter shows that alignment being built at staff level. Senior aides exchanged views before any summit could decide policy.
frus-1944-quebec-d174:
Another luncheon at Quebec left no official record, and the editors again rely on Mackenzie King's notes. The conversation ranged widely: the Soviet position toward Japan after the European war, conditions in India, the instability of French governments, and the United States Constitution all came up. So did the race problem in South Africa and the entry of troops into Berlin and Vienna.

De Gaulle, a possible civil war in France, and China also figured in the talk. After luncheon, the party moved to the conference room at the Citadel. There Churchill demonstrated models of the ships and equipment used to form the artificial harbors for the invasion of France. The note preserves the texture of a working lunch at the summit.
frus-1944-quebec-d274:
The Japan section of the draft final report, C.C.S. 680 of September 14, 1944, states the agreed objective and the operations accepted for planning. Japan's unconditional surrender would be forced by blockade, bombardment, and destruction of her air and naval strength, then by invading her industrial heart. Plans were to stay flexible and exploit naval and air superiority, avoiding costly land campaigns where possible.

The schedule runs from Talaud in October 1944 to the Tokyo Plain in December 1945, by way of Leyte and either Formosa or Luzon. Very-long-range bombers would strike Japan from China and the Marianas. The report also records agreement that the British Fleet should join the main operations, balanced and self-supporting.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d74:
Voting procedure in the Security Council is the whole subject of this 15 November 1944 memorandum to the President. Acting Secretary Stettinius lays out where each great power stood after Dumbarton Oaks. The paper belongs to the set prepared for a White House meeting and printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Three issues are in dispute: the size of the majority, whether permanent members must agree, and whether a member involved in a dispute may vote. The Russians wanted a simple majority but a veto that applied even to parties in a dispute. The British and Chinese wanted a two-thirds majority and no vote for disputing parties. The American delegation, by the President's instructions, stood close to the British.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d174:
Ambassador Richard Patterson sent Washington the Tito–Subasic agreements on 16 December 1944. Writing from London, where the Yugoslav exile government sat, he reports that Premier Subasic handed him translations of the texts that day. His despatch is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Four papers are enclosed. First comes the main agreement of 1 November 1944 between Subasic and Marshal Tito. Two supplemental agreements of 7 December follow. One covers elections for a constituent assembly and the ordering of public powers. The other treats the King's property and a regency council. A communiqué of the same date completes the set. Patterson warns that the wording is far from precise in places, and leaves wide room for differing readings.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d274:
Moscow named its negotiators on prisoners on 29 December 1944. Harriman's short confidential cable to the Secretary of State, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, reports a letter from Deputy Commissar Vyshinsky. It follows Molotov's note on two-way repatriation of the month before.

Lieutenant General K. D. Golubev and Major General N. V. Slavin, Vyshinsky writes, have been appointed by the Soviet government. They will conduct negotiations with General Deane. The subject is the plan to repatriate, each to his own country, American and Soviet prisoners of war and civilians. The principles are those set out in Molotov's letter to Kennan of 25 November. Losers in the game, the five Pandava brothers accept thirteen years of exile. Stories within stories fill the long forest years, since the epic pauses for tales of gods, kings, and lovers. Ganguli's Victorian prose moves steadily through it all. The longest poem in world literature opens here, with every thread of the coming war in place.
tob-9052-15474:
Ganguli's complete English Mahabharata begins, in this copy, with the epic's opening movement. Two branches of the Kuru house grow up rivals. A dice game, fixed against the honest Pandava brothers, strips them of kingdom, wealth, and freedom in one disastrous hall scene.

Sentenced to thirteen years of exile, the brothers withdraw to the forest. The long banishment fills with adventures, disguises, and tales told to pass the years. Every insult stays remembered; every debt will be called in. Readers meet the vast cast slowly, which suits a poem of this scale. The fuse for the great war is lit here, and it burns through the whole epic.
tob-13329-15474:
Books one to three of the Mahabharata open Ganguli's translation in its Vyasa-titled copy. The Kuru kings rise, marry, and quarrel. A dice game in the royal hall, played with loaded stakes, costs the Pandava brothers their kingdom and sends them into the forest.

Thirteen years of exile follow, full of demons, pilgrimages, and stories nested inside stories. The brothers gather allies and grievances in equal measure. Ganguli, the first to render the whole epic into English prose, keeps the huge cast straight. Every feud that drives the later war is planted here, in the longest story ever told.

Julian Morgenstern, a scholar of the Hebrew Bible, turned his tools on Babylon for a study of how its people understood sin. Mesopotamia's temples kept rites for guilt, stain, and cleansing long before Israel's psalms. Morgenstern reads those rites closely in an early work of comparative religion.

He describes confession, sorrowful hymns, and the fear that a hidden fault had angered a god. Priests acted as healers of both body and conscience, since sin and sickness blurred together. The study shows an old moral world in fine detail. Readers of the Bible will meet many echoes of its ideas next door in Babylon.
tob-9174:
Budge compiled his Egyptian Hieroglyphic Dictionary as the key to the carved and painted writings of ancient Egypt. Sign lists and vast word lists fill its volumes, the fruit of his decades at the British Museum. Generations of pupils learned to read the glyphs from Budge's pages.

The dictionary's learning is very much of the 1800s, and later Egyptology corrected it in many places. Its scale, though, commands respect: thousands of words gathered before modern corpora existed. Checked from the 1919 printing, the work stands as a high point of early Egypt lore and a tool that opened tombs and temples to readers.
tob-10274:
The Book of Jubilees retells Genesis and the start of Exodus as a secret account given to Moses by angels. It was written in Hebrew in the second century BC, most likely. R. H. Charles edited and translated the surviving text, which came down whole in Ethiopic.

The story is divided into blocks of forty-nine years, the jubilees that give the book its name. It adds detail on angels, the calendar, and laws it says the patriarchs already kept. The Ethiopian church counts it as scripture, while other churches treat it as apocrypha. It helps show how Jews of its age read the Bible.
smyth-our-inheritance-great-pyramid-1874:
Astronomer Charles Piazzi Smyth argued that the Great Pyramid hides divine measure and prophecy. His book Our Inheritance in the Great Pyramid first appeared in 1864. Smyth held Scotland's top post in astronomy.

He claims a sacred pyramid inch guides the building's design. Chambers and passages, he says, map sacred history in stone. His charts and numbers fill page after page. Fellow scientists mostly rejected the scheme. Yet the book launched pyramid prophecy as a lasting genre. It is a curious, earnest work from an age when faith and science still shared one desk.
crookes-researches-phenomena-spiritualis:
Sir William Crookes, one of Britain's leading chemists and physicists, published his Researches in the Phenomena of Spiritualism in 1874. The text here follows the 1926 reprint, which adds his 1898 address and an appendix by Arthur Conan Doyle. Crookes brought lab habits into the séance room.

He reports tests on famous mediums, above all D. D. Home and Kate Fox. Under his watches and scales, tables moved, sounds came, and forms seemed to appear. Crookes would not call the force spirits, but he said the facts were real. The book still fuels debate on science and belief.
dawkins-cave-hunting-1874:
W. Boyd Dawkins, a geologist and cave explorer, published Cave Hunting in 1874. The book synthesizes the cave archaeology of his generation: what caves hold about the early inhabitants of Europe. Dawkins dug many of the sites himself, above all in Britain.

He shows human tools and bones lying with the remains of mammoth, hyena, and reindeer in cave earth. From that company he argues the great antiquity of man in Britain. Caves in France, Germany, and Belgium extend the case. The synthesis was bold for 1874 and has been much revised since. It marks the moment cave evidence became central to the human story.
northampton-assizes-relation-1674:
Mary Forster stood trial at the Northampton assizes in 1674, and a relation of the proceedings keeps her case. Relation of the Proceedings at the Northampton Assizes prints the charge, her confession as reported, and her death. The trial falls in the Restoration years, well past the Civil War.

By 1674 many in England doubted witch charges, yet the courts still heard them and still hanged. Forster's case shows the old charge at work in a new and more wary age. The report is short, plain, and sad in the usual way of these prints. It proves the gallows for witches had not yet closed.
randolph-eulis-1874:
Paschal Beverly Randolph set out his most fought claim in Eulis!, his book of 1874. He held that the act of love, rightly used, is a rite of great force. Through it the soul can heal, see, and draw near to God. He taught this lore in hid groups for years ere he dared print it.

The print caused shock and rows at once. Yet his lore spread, by hid paths, to bands in the West for years. This book is the turn point of his life's work. It still sparks awe and doubt in kind. His heirs in hid bands kept the book in print by hand. That care shows how much weight his close fans gave these bold claims.
wallace-defence-modern-spiritualism-1874:
Alfred Russel Wallace first spoke out for the faith in A Defence of Modern Spiritualism, a brief tract of 1874. Foes had mocked his faith in the dark room in the press. Wallace, a famed man of science, replies in calm print. He sums the proof as he sees it and asks for a fair test, not scorn.

The tract is short, clear, and brave for its day. It came ere his fat book of 1878 on the same theme. Here is the first time a top name in science stood up in print for the seance.
steller-kamchatka-1774:
Georg Wilhelm Steller sailed as naturalist on Vitus Bering's last voyage to the Pacific, and his account of Kamchatka came out in German in 1774. He died on the trip home, so the book came out years after his death. Kamchatka is the wild far east coast of Siberia.

Steller wrote of the land, its beasts and plants, and the Itelmen people who lived there. He gave the first account by a trained eye of Itelmen shamans and their rites. The book first opened that remote coast to European science. His notes on the great sea cow are still prized as well.
priestley-experiments-observations-air-1:
Joseph Priestley, an English cleric and keen chemist, brought out this set of trials on air in three parts from 1774 to 1777. He worked with lenses, troughs of water, and mice in sealed jars. His lab was a plain room, yet the gains were huge.

Priestley made and named a string of new gases, one by one. The most famed was the pure air we now call oxygen, which he named dephlogisticated air. Odd as it sounds, he held to the phlogiston scheme all his life, while his finds broke it.
darwin-descent-of-man-2nd-ed-1874:
Charles Darwin published The Descent of Man in 1871, and the 1874 second edition is his revised, fuller text. In it he applies his theory of evolution to human beings. He also adds a long study of sexual selection in animals and man.

Darwin argues that humans share ancestors with other animals. He points to body structure, early growth, and shared traits as proof. Sexual selection, he says, shaped traits from bird song to human looks. The book caused fierce debate and still anchors talks on human origins. He revised with care as new facts and letters arrived.
valera-pepita-jimenez-1874:
Juan Valera published Pepita Jimenez in 1874, a Spanish novel told mostly in letters. Luis de Vargas is a young man training for the priesthood. He returns to his village and meets Pepita, a young and charming widow. His letters to his uncle trace a growing love he feels he must resist.

The clash between duty and desire drives the whole story. Valera writes with warmth and gentle humor about faith, family, and small-town life. Pepita is no mere temptress but a strong and thoughtful woman. The English text here dates from 1886. The novel remains Valera's best-known work in any language.
verne-mysterious-island-1874:
Jules Verne published The Mysterious Island in 1874, a novel about five men cast away during the American Civil War. They escape by balloon and land on an unknown island in the Pacific. Led by the engineer Cyrus Smith, they build tools, a home, and even a telegraph. Almost nothing on the island is wasted.

Strange help arrives at key moments, and the men sense a hidden presence. Late in the book the source of that help is revealed, linking this story to Captain Nemo. The Kingston translation is the text given here. Readers value the novel as a hymn to skill, science, and teamwork.
alarcon-three-cornered-hat-1874:
Pedro Antonio de Alarcon published The Three-Cornered Hat in 1874, a Spanish tale set in a small Andalusian town. Lucas is a miller whose wife, Frasquita, is admired by the town's mayor, or corregidor. The corregidor, named for his three-cornered hat, plots to have Lucas sent away for a night. He hopes to visit Frasquita alone.

Frasquita outwits him, and a chain of mix-ups in the dark follows. Husbands, wives, and officials trade places and chase each other through the night. Alarcon based the story on an old folk ballad. Its humor and pace later inspired a famous ballet with music by Manuel de Falla.
hardy-far-from-madding-1874:
Thomas Hardy published Far from the Madding Crowd in 1874, a novel set in his Wessex countryside. Bathsheba Everdene inherits a farm and runs it herself, to local surprise. Three men seek her hand: the steady shepherd Gabriel Oak, the bold farmer Boldwood, and the dashing Sergeant Troy. Her choices bring joy and harm in turn.

Oak works for Bathsheba in silence after his own losses. Troy's charm hides a faithless past that returns to haunt the parish. Harvests, storms, and fairs mark the seasons of the tale. Hardy writes with love for rural work and custom. The book was his first great success.
draper-conflict-religion-science-1874:
John William Draper published History of the Conflict between Religion and Science in 1874. Draper, an American scientist and historian, states the conflict thesis in classic form. Science and faith, he argues, have fought through the ages, and faith's rule has stalled progress. He surveys astronomy, geology, medicine, and the theory of evolution.

Draper aimed much of his fire at the Catholic Church of his day. His history is vivid, learned, and partisan in equal measure. The book defined the science and religion debate for a century. Later historians have shown the real story to be more tangled. Even so, Draper's volume remains the thesis's arsenal and a key text.
stubbs-constitutional-history-vol-1-1874:
William Stubbs published The Constitutional History of England, Volume 1, in 1874. Stubbs, a bishop and Oxford historian, founded English constitutional history as a discipline. This volume runs from the Anglo-Saxon settlements to the death of Richard I. He traces shires, courts, kingship, and the Norman settlement in fine detail.

Stubbs built his account from charters, chronicles, and law codes at first hand. His framework, often called Stubbsian, guided scholars for generations. Later research corrected his love of Teutonic origins and free assemblies. Even so, the mastery of sources still commands respect. The three volumes remain a monument of Victorian scholarship.
justinian-institutes-sandars-1874:
Thomas Collett Sandars published his translation of The Institutes of Justinian in this 1874 form, first issued in 1853. Justinian I, the Byzantine emperor, had the Institutes made in 533 CE as the student part of his great codification of Roman law. Generations of law students began with it.

The Institutes teach the elements of law: persons, property, contracts, wrongs, and actions, in short and ordered rules. Behind them stood the full mass of Roman legal writing that Justinian's teams had sorted. The work became the foundation of civil-law systems across Europe and beyond. Sandars's English, the standard student version, keeps the clarity that made the original a textbook for over a thousand years.
cyril-commentary-john-pusey-1874:
Cyril of Alexandria, the fifth-century patriarch, read the Gospel of John as the great proof of his teaching on Christ. His commentary covers the whole gospel in twelve books. P. E. Pusey translated the first volume in 1874, and Thomas Randell finished the work in 1885 for the Library of the Fathers.

Verse by verse, Cyril draws out the claim that the Word is true God and truly became man. He fights the Arian reading of John at every turn, and he feeds the reader moral counsel as he goes. The commentary shows the Alexandrian school at its most intense. It shaped how the Greek church read John for a thousand years.
brentano-psychologie-empirischen-standpu:
Franz Brentano published his Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint at Vienna in 1874, and modern thought on the mind starts there. The text here is the German first edition, complete as issued. No English version in the public domain exists. Brentano had been a priest and a professor, and he wrote to put psychology on firm ground.

His key claim is that every mental act points at an object: we believe something, love something, judge something. That pointing, which he named intentionality, became the seed of phenomenology through his pupil Husserl. The book also shaped the study of mind in the analytic line. It stands in German as a founding record.
retz-memoirs-1774:
Jean François Paul de Gondi, Cardinal de Retz, wrote his Mémoires about the Fronde, the revolt that shook France in his youth. Retz was no bystander: he plotted, preached, and intrigued at the center of the rising against the young Louis XIV's court. The memoirs were first published in 1717, and the English translation of 1774 fills this text.

Retz tells his story with unmatched wit, candor about his own ambition, and a gambler's love of the game. He judges allies and enemies alike with a cool, amused eye. French readers rank the book among the most brilliant memoirs ever written. Its cynicism is matched only by its sparkle, page after page.
hegel-logic-wallace-1874:
William Wallace translated Hegel's Encyclopaedia Logic into English in 1874, giving British readers their classic Hegel. The German work first appeared in 1817 as part one of Hegel's Encyclopaedia system. Scholars call it the lesser Logic, to mark it from his larger logic book. Its subject is pure thought itself.

Hegel moves through three great stages: being, essence, and notion. Each stage shows a basic form of thought giving way to a richer one. The path is hard, yet Wallace's version guided generations of students. Readers meet here the engine of Hegel's whole system. Everything else he wrote builds on it.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
Timothy Field Allen aimed at completeness, and his Encyclopaedia of Pure Materia Medica began in 1874. Volume I opens a record meant to hold every symptom from every prover, sorted by remedy. Allen, a New York doctor and botanist, gathered reports from across the homeopathic world.

Nothing is summed up or sharpened here; the raw proving record stands as reported. That choice made the set the largest homeopathic materia medica ever compiled, a quarry for later, shorter books. Kent and others mined these pages. The first volume sets the scale: exact, vast, and meant for reference, not reading through.

Volume II of Allen's Encyclopaedia, also from 1874, keeps the great proving record moving at full pace. Timothy Field Allen collected symptoms from every source he trusted, then filed each one under its remedy. The order within an entry runs through the body, region by region, so nothing hides.

Allen prints what provers said, in their own plain terms, with sources named beside the reports. A reader can watch one drug act across dozens of people, dose by dose and day by day. As the second of ten volumes, it deepens the archive that made the Encyclopaedia the school's fullest store of drug effects.
livingstone-last-journals-vol1-1874:
David Livingstone, the Scottish missionary and explorer, kept journals on his final African expedition from 1866 until his death. Volume One of The Last Journals, edited by Horace Waller in 1874, prints that closing record. Livingstone's porters carried the books out after he died at Ilala.

Weakened by fever and bleeding, Livingstone pressed on around Lakes Tanganyika and Bangweulu, still hunting the Nile's source. He records slave caravans and his horror at the trade's cruelties. Waller adds letters and a narrative of the last days. The volume is both a travel record and a testament of endurance.
livingstone-last-journals-vol2-1874:
Volume Two of Livingstone's Last Journals completes the record of his final expedition, 1866 to 1873. Horace Waller edited the notebooks that Livingstone's faithful servants saved. The explorer's body itself was carried to the coast for return to Britain.

The entries grow sparser as illness and hardship mount, yet the observations on land, people, and the slave trade stay sharp. Waller's narrative fills gaps with accounts from those who were there. The story ends with Livingstone found dead, kneeling by his bed in prayer. Few exploration books carry such emotional weight alongside their geography. Waller's preface explains how the notebooks were saved and sorted.
stanley-coomassie-magdala-1874:
Henry Stanley reported two British campaigns in Africa for the New York Herald before he was famous as an explorer. Coomassie and Magdala, from 1874, gathers his dispatches from the Abyssinian campaign and the Ashanti expedition of 1873 and 1874. The reporting made his name.

Stanley marches with the troops to Magdala, where Emperor Theodore died, and into the Ashanti capital, Coomassie. He writes fast, vivid copy about heat, disease, and battle. The book shows a war correspondent inventing his own legend on the march. It is also a raw record of Britain's small, brutal African wars. His Herald editors printed the pieces first for American readers hungry for war news.
schweinfurth-heart-africa-vol1-1874:
Georg Schweinfurth, a German botanist, traveled the Bahr el Ghazal region of the Sudan from 1868 to 1871. Volume One of The Heart of Africa, from 1874, reports his route into lands then unknown to Europeans. He went for plants and stayed for the peoples.

Schweinfurth describes the river systems, the ivory trade, and the peoples of the region, including the Niam-niam, wrongly feared as cannibals. His plant collections were vast, and his maps fixed a blank space on the chart. He writes with a scientist's care and a traveler's relish. The volume opened the upper Nile country to European knowledge.
schweinfurth-heart-africa-vol2-1874:
Volume Two of Schweinfurth's Heart of Africa completes his three years in the unexplored Sudan. The botanist-explorer pushed south toward the Congo watershed. What he found there made the book famous across Europe.

He meets the Monbuttoo, with their fine crafts and great hall, and the Akka, a pygmy people of the forest. Schweinfurth gives the first reliable report of pygmies in the Congo basin. He also condemns the slave and ivory raids ruining the region. His return journey closes the work. Few African travel books of the age join science and story so well.
plos-pone-0003474:
Feng Cao and co-authors profiled lab-grown heart cells in this 2008 paper. Human embryonic stem cells can become cardiomyocytes, the beating cells of heart muscle. Such cells might one day repair hearts hurt by ischemia, or low blood flow. The team studied the cells' gene activity and function together.

Their portrait shows what these stem cell products can and cannot do. Gene profiles and behavior tests mark how mature the cells are. That detail matters before any use in patients. The study helps set checks for future heart cell therapies. Heart failure is common and deadly, so even partial repair would help many.
plos-pone-0003574:
Guisheng Song and Li Wang untangled two small RNA genes in this 2008 paper. MicroRNAs help control development, metabolism, and cancer growth. Little was known about their primary transcripts and gene control. The pair miR-433 and miR-127 share one genomic locus.

The team cloned two primary transcripts, one for each microRNA. The transcripts overlap, yet arise independently of each other. Two regulators can thus be read from the same crowded address separately. Sorting that out clarifies how this neighborhood is controlled. Tiny RNAs like these are now tracked as markers in blood tests for cancer.
plos-pone-0003674:
Thomas F. Wierzba, Ibrahim Adib Abdel-Messih, Bayoumi Gharib, and colleagues published this neurology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Guillain-Barré syndrome is a sudden immune attack on the nerves that can leave people weak or paralyzed. Campylobacter, a common foodborne gut germ, is a known trigger elsewhere.

Working in Egypt, the team tested whether Campylobacter infection also sets the syndrome off there. Linking a routine gut infection to a rare nerve disease matters for both diagnosis and food safety. The study adds Egyptian evidence to the case that this bacterium can start the body's attack on its own nerves.
plos-pone-0003774:
Jingui Ma, Xianliang Xin, Linghua Meng, and colleagues published this cancer drug study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Drugs that block several tyrosine kinases at once have shown promise against tumors. Side effects and resistance remain concerns. The team tested a marine-derived compound, an oligosaccharide sulfate called MdOS.

MdOS blocked multiple tyrosine kinases and fought tumor angiogenesis, the growth of new blood vessels that feed tumors. It worked both in cell tests and in living animals. The compound joins the hunt for multi-target cancer drugs with fewer side effects and less resistance.
plos-pone-0003874:
Dominik Seelow, Jana Marie Schwarz, and Markus Schuelke presented a software tool called GeneDistiller in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article addresses a common problem in gene hunting. Studies that track traits through families often narrow the search to a stretch of DNA. That stretch can still hold several hundred genes.

GeneDistiller helps users rank those genes by how likely each is to cause a disease. It draws together data that researchers once gathered by hand. Manual searches stay flexible, but they take much time over large lists. The tool gives gene hunters a short list of strong leads to test first in the lab.
plos-pone-0003974:
Cedrick D. Dotson, Lan Zhang, Hong Xu, and co-authors studied bitter taste receptors beyond the tongue in 2008. Taste receptors of the TAS2R type detect bitter compounds. They also appear in cells lining the mammalian gut. There they help the body handle nutrients it takes in.

Their PLOS ONE article reports bitter receptors influence glucose balance. Gut sensing of bitter compounds may adjust sugar handling after meals. That role links taste machinery to metabolism and diabetes risk. Drugs aimed at these receptors might one day help control blood sugar. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004074:
Fiona M. Brandie, Veronica Aran, Avani Verma, and co-authors studied membrane fusion control in fat and muscle cells in 2008. Insulin moves the glucose transporter GLUT4 to the cell surface. That move raises glucose uptake into fat and muscle. It is a specialized form of controlled membrane fusion.

Their PLOS ONE article reports Munc18c restrains that fusion process in vitro. The fusion uses syntaxin4, SNAP-23, and VAMP2 proteins. A brake on fusion keeps glucose uptake off until insulin calls. Understanding the brake helps explain insulin resistance at cell level. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004174:
Jürgen Löhler and colleagues published this protein mapping study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Casein kinase 1 delta, or CK1δ, adds phosphate tags to many key proteins. Through them it touches cell growth, specialisation, cell death, the daily body clock, and transport inside cells. Faults in this kinase have also been linked to diseases of the degenerating brain.

Using antibody staining, the team charted which cell types in young adult BALB/c mice actually make CK1δ, tissue by tissue. A map of where a busy kinase works is basic knowledge for judging what goes wrong when it fails.
plos-pone-0004274:
Michael Allemand and colleagues published this study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS, combines excess male hormones with frequent insulin resistance in skeletal muscle. The team asked whether testosterone itself worsens insulin action in muscle cells.

Working with primary rat muscle tubes grown in the lab, they tested whether testosterone increases serine phosphorylation of IRS1, a change that blunts insulin signalling. Their setup offers a potential model for PCOS-related insulin resistance. If a hormone drives the resistance directly, treatments could target that link. PCOS is one of the most common hormone disorders in women.
plos-pone-0004374:
Doctors often must decide for patients who cannot speak for themselves. One rule for those choices is substituted judgment, deciding as the patient would have decided. Farr Curlin, Ryan Lawrence, and Julie Fredrickson studied how well new medical students grasp that rule. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper followed a course on clinical ethics.

Students wrote essays on one of three hard cases given in class. The authors read those essays for signs of true understanding. Their title asks whether the students' grasp was an ethical facade. The paper shows future doctors can sound right while missing the point. That gap matters for how ethics courses should be taught.
plos-pone-0004474: In 2009, Yang, Wang, and Gregory read a family's troubled genome. The genomic landscape of a rare three-generation pedigree with affective disorder was mapped. The bipolar family's DNA was charted. The study aids psychiatric genetics greatly. The pedigree was remarkably rare.
plos-pone-0004574: In 2009, Liu and a team found low dopamine making male flies hot to males. Reduced dopamine raised male Drosophila attractiveness to other males. The brain chemical tuned courtship moves. The finding maps brain tuning of desire. The test flies were mutant.
plos-pone-0004674: In 2009, White and Erickson compared chromosome-gluing coils across many species. Cohesin coiled coils proved conserved in animals but not yeast. The SMC proteins' coils differed widely. The neat finding maps chromosome biology anew. The long coils are anti-parallel.
plos-pone-0004774: In 2009, a team found hunger drugs fighting cancer wasting anew here. Pill-form hunger blockers made subjects eat more and waste less. The mice ate more daily indeed. The study maps hunger drug research. The wasting illness is body-wide indeed.
zola-conquest-plassans-1874:
Chatto and Windus issued The Conquest of Plassans at London in 1917, in Vizetelly's English version. Twenty-two chapters carry the tale in the fourth Rougon-Macquart volume. The scene returns to Plassans, the small town where the family saga began.

A smiling young priest, Abbe Faujas, arrives and slowly takes hold of the town. His grip tightens on the sound Mouret household, which becomes his tool. Faith curdles into fanatic drive as ambition conquers from within. The tale ends in madness and fire, by the v1 account. Dark and tense, it ranks among the most gripping volumes of the whole cycle.
cairnes-leading-principles-1874:
Cairnes published Some Leading Principles of Political Economy Newly Expounded in 1874, his restatement of the classical creed. He wrote as the old Ricardian system was coming under strain and a new economics of marginal utility was gathering force. The book defends the old faith by arguing it afresh, not by merely repeating it.

Its three parts treat value, wages and profits, and trade between nations. Cairnes refines the labor theory of value and gives a famous account of how wages are set when groups of workers cannot compete freely. The writing is exact and unadorned. Historians often call the book the last great statement of the classical school, the old economics at its best just before the subject changed direction.
walras-elements-vol1-1874:
Léon Walras published the first part of his Elements of Pure Political Economy in French in 1874. Walras, teaching at Lausanne, aimed to do for economics what Newton had done for physics: state the whole system in exact, mathematical form. The first part lays the foundation with his theory of exchange.

He shows how prices form when many traders, each seeking the most satisfaction, meet in one market. From two traders and two goods he builds toward the general case, the whole economy balanced in a system of equations. Value, on his account, comes from scarcity joined to usefulness. The book founded general equilibrium theory, the idea that all markets clear together. Economics became a mathematical science in these pages, though the world took decades to notice.
walras-elements-vol2-1874:
The second part of Walras's Elements of Pure Political Economy followed the first in French in 1874. Part 1 had built the theory of exchange between traders. Part 2 works out the system in full, extending the equations to production, capital, and money.

Walras treats capital goods as sources of services that earn rent, and money as the good in which accounts are kept. His famous device of an auctioneer crying prices until supply meets demand shows how equilibrium could be found in practice. The mathematics scared off many early readers, and the book's fame grew slowly. By the mid-twentieth century it was honored as the most exact statement of the marginal revolution. The Lausanne master's complete theory stands in these two parts.
cia-0000009874:
The status of imprisoned American pilots in the Sam Neua area of Houa Phan province is assessed in a July 1966 item. Sam Neua's cave country held some of the earliest American captives of the Laos war. A status report asks the basic questions: how many, how held, how faring.

Early status reports set the baseline for everything filed later about these men. If the 1966 picture was wrong, later files inherited the error. Analysts therefore wrote them with unusual care on thin evidence. This item preserves that baseline for the Sam Neua pilots, the forgotten front's first prisoners.
cia-0000010474:
Iranian and Middle East oil, and its importance to Western Europe in peacetime and beyond, fill a January 1951 CIA paper. The heading's final words are cut short, but the subject is clear: oil as the West's lifeline. Europe's recovery ran on Middle Eastern crude moved through few chokepoints.

The paper weighs how much Europe depended on that oil and what interruption would do. Months later, Iran's oil nationalization turned the study into front-page crisis. Analysts had stated the stakes in advance, in writing. This file preserves that warning, a resource study that reads like a forecast of the decade.
cia-0000010774:
By 1960, oil from the Middle East powered much of the world's economy. That October the CIA surveyed the region's petroleum in a single paper written at the height of the Cold War. Western oil companies still ran most of the fields, but the producing states were pressing for a larger share of the wealth.

The survey covers the size of the reserves, the companies that pumped the oil, and the politics around both. It treats oil as a strategic prize that shaped alliances and rivalries across the region. For readers, it lays out why control of these fields mattered so much to Washington.
cia-0000012274:
In March 1962 a letter passed hand to hand through cutouts, and the CIA file holds its translation. The title notes the transfer date, March 28, 1962, with the names of those involved blanked out. The letter belongs to the Penkovsky operation's late phase, when the Soviet colonel's meetings abroad had ended and contact ran through riskier channels.

Mercier had served in Washington since 1860 and knew the capital's politics at close range.
frus-1862-d474:
A second instruction of the same date, 9 July 1862, went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to James E. Harvey in Lisbon. It is Document 474 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed beside its companion.

Two orders on one day usually meant two separate subjects, each kept in its own letter as the Department's practice required. For Lisbon in 1862 the standing subjects were neutral-port rules, Confederate attempts to use Portuguese waters, and the safety of American trade. Harvey needed clear lines on all of them. Paired with the previous document, this instruction shows how the paperwork of neutrality was built: one question, one letter, one clear answer from Washington.
frus-1862-d574:
A second instruction of 12 December 1861 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to James Watson Webb in Rio de Janeiro. It stands as Document 574 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, beside its same-day companion.

Paired orders meant paired subjects, kept separate by the Department's one-question practice. For Brazil in that December the questions were wide. They ran from the treatment of belligerent ships in Brazilian ports to the presentation of the Union's cause. That cause had to be put across South America. Webb, a forceful personality, was not a man to leave instructions unexecuted. The two letters together give the reader the whole of Washington's December brief for its most distant major post in the Americas.
frus-1862-d674:
Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this letter to Anson Burlingame on 2 April 1862. Burlingame was the American minister to China, half a world from Washington. The letter stands as document 674 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Orders sent to China had to be broad, since months passed before an answer could come back. Seward's letters therefore set aims and limits, then trusted the envoy on the spot. This one falls in the spring run of the China file, between Burlingame's reports of March and May. It shows the trust, and the strain, built into running foreign ties by sail and steamer.
frus-1863p1-d74:
From the London legation on 6 February 1863, Charles Francis Adams sent dispatch number 316 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 74 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

In it, Adams sent Washington a copy of the Queen's speech at the opening of Parliament the day before. The speech said Britain's ties with foreign powers stayed warm. It said the Queen had held back from any step to stop the fight in North America. For Seward, that was the news that counted: Britain would not step in. The letter is a small hinge in the file, proof on paper of British calm.
frus-1863p1-d174:
April closed at the London legation with this dispatch from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 30 April 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 174 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is the last of the run in this part of the file.

Adams closed April with a report from the post he had made the Union's shield in Europe. His spring mail had charted Britain's turn on the ships and the slow fade of the South's hopes there. This dispatch is a fitting tail to the run: one more cool, exact sheet from London. The file goes on past it, but the spring's story is whole in these pages.
frus-1863p1-d274:
A dispatch dated 27 August 1863 carried news from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 274 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

The CSS Alabama, built in a British yard, had escaped to sea in 1862 and was burning Union merchant ships. London's handling of such ships hung over every report Adams sent home. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d374:
One entry in the running Washington exchange, this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, is dated 28 January 1863. It stands as document 374 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

After the Emancipation Proclamation in January 1863, Seward could frame the war as a fight against slavery. That put Britain, which had banned slavery at home, in an awkward spot when it aided the South. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d474:
Under the date 23 April 1863, the record holds a letter from Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d574:
Document 574, dated 19 June 1863, records a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d674:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 23 November 1863 letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
plos-pbio-0000074:
Alexei A. Sharov, Yulan Piao, Ryo Matoba, and co-workers charted gene activity in mouse stem cells for PLOS Biology in 2003. They measured which genes are switched on in stem cells and in very early embryos. Such a full survey is called a transcriptome analysis.

Stem cells can turn into many cell types, and genes switched on or off drive that choice. A clear list of active genes gives a baseline for spotting what keeps a cell flexible and what pushes it to mature. The data set became a shared tool for other labs. It helps compare cell lines, test culture methods, and hunt for the core genes of early development.
plos-pbio-0020174:
David R. Halpin and Pehr B. Harbury continued their DNA display series with part two in PLOS Biology in 2004. The first part showed how to route DNA pools by sequence. This part shows how to apply genetic tricks, like mutation and selection, to libraries of chemical compounds tagged with DNA.

Treating a chemical library like a population of genes lets researchers breed better compounds over rounds of selection. Weak binders are washed away, winners are copied, and the cycle repeats. That evolution in a test tube can find strong drug leads from huge starting pools. The paper sets out the rules for copying and varying the library without losing track of which DNA tag means which compound.
plos-pbio-0020274:
Eugene Hur, Samuel J. Pfaff, E. Sturgis Payne, and their team studied the androgen receptor in PLOS Biology in 2004. This receptor responds to male hormones and switches genes on with the help of partner proteins called coactivators. The partners dock onto a specific surface of the receptor.

The study shows how the receptor reshapes that docking surface to fit its partners, a process the title calls recognition and accommodation. A clear view of the fit matters for prostate disease, where this receptor is a main drug target. Drugs that block the docking site could work where current hormone blockers fail. The paper gives that search a firm structural base.
plos-pone-0000074:
Ines Van Bocxlaer, Kim Roelants, S. D. Biju, and a large team traced frog history in PLOS ONE in 2006. Gondwana was the ancient southern supercontinent that split into Africa, South America, India, and other lands. Frog groups found across those lands may have been carried apart as the continent broke, a process called vicariance.

Their genetic timelines fit a Late Cretaceous split, matching the continent's breakup. That match means the frogs' spread was set by geology, not by later ocean crossings. Old frogs are poor swimmers over salt water, so the vicariance story makes sense. The paper is a clean case of using DNA clocks to test a geological story.
plos-pone-0000174:
Jennifer L. Baxter-Roshek, Alexey N. Petrov, and Jonathan D. Dinman published this molecular biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Ribosomes, the machines that build proteins, are themselves built from RNA and protein. The authors study how chemical modifications to ribosomal RNA bases fine-tune the ribosome's structure and function.

Those small chemical marks can change how accurately and how fast proteins are made. The authors review and test the optimization these modifications provide. Because antibiotics often target ribosomes, and because faulty ribosomes cause disease, understanding this tuning has use well beyond basic biology.
plos-pone-0000274:
Kirsten E. Nicholson, Luke J. Harmon, and Jonathan B. Losos published this lizard evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Anolis lizards carry a dewlap, a flap of skin under the throat that males flash in display. Its color and pattern vary richly between species. The authors study the evolution of that dewlap diversity across the Anolis group.

Dewlaps are signals, used to claim territory and attract mates, so their variety may track how species recognize their own kind. The authors test patterns in that diversity against the lizards' history. The work is part of a famous research program using Anolis as a model of adaptive radiation.
plos-pone-0000374:
Marion Coolen and colleagues used a shark relative to study how body plans evolved, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. All jawed vertebrates, from fish to humans, build their bodies along a head-to-tail axis using inherited genetic programs. The team asked how those axis-setting programs changed as jawed vertebrates evolved.

Chondrichthyans, the group that includes sharks and skates, split early from other jawed vertebrates, so their development preserves clues about the ancestral state. Comparing their axis-forming mechanisms with those of other animals shows which parts of the program are ancient and which are new. The work helps explain how a shared body plan diversified across half a billion years.
plos-pone-0000474:
Sofie Ignoul and colleagues characterized a little-known human chloride channel protein, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The protein, ClC-6, is a glycoprotein found in late endosomes, sorting compartments inside cells. The team also reported that it associates with detergent-resistant lipid domains, the membrane patches known as lipid rafts.

Members of the ClC family move chloride ions and help set the chemistry inside cell compartments; faults in relatives cause kidney and bone disease. Placing ClC-6 in late endosomes and in raft domains narrows down what it likely does. Basic placement work like this precedes any understanding of a protein's role in health and disease.
plos-pone-0000574:
Christopher C. Hemond, Nancy G. Kanwisher, and Hans P. Op de Beeck reported a spatial bias in the brain's object areas, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Human cortex contains regions that respond strongly to objects and faces. The team found a preference for contralateral stimuli in that cortex. In plain terms, each side of the brain favors sights from the opposite side of view.

A contralateral bias is expected in early vision but was less charted in high-level areas that supposedly see the whole scene. Showing the bias persists there reshapes how researchers read brain scans of recognition. It also bears on patients with one-sided brain damage, whose neglect of one side of space may start in these regions.
plos-pone-0000674:
Athanasios G. Michos, Vassiliki P. Syriopoulou, Christos Hadjichristodoulou and colleagues reviewed 506 cases of aseptic meningitis in children for PLOS ONE in 2007. Aseptic meningitis is inflammation of the membranes around the brain without a bacterial cause. Non-polio human enteroviruses are its leading cause in children. A PCR test can spot enterovirus directly.

The role of that PCR test in diagnosis and management had not been fully explored. In a look-back study of past cases, the team gathered epidemiological, clinical, and laboratory details. Patterns across 506 cases can show which children need the test, and how results change care and hospital stays.
plos-pone-0000774:
Elisabetta Mattei, Nicoletta Corbi, Maria Grazia Di Certo and colleagues tried a gene-therapy route for Duchenne muscular dystrophy in mice. DMD is a severe muscle degenerative disease caused by absence of the protein dystrophin. No treatment yet works, as the authors state. Their aim was to raise levels of utrophin, a related gene, to complement the missing dystrophin.

They used an artificial transcription factor, a built protein meant to switch the utrophin gene up. In transgenic mice, the factor up-regulated utrophin as intended. Substituting a stand-in protein is a clever strategy when the original gene is too large or too broken to replace directly.
plos-pone-0000874:
Jonathan Aldridge, Tomohisa Horibe and Nicholas Hoogenraad hunted for genes switched on by the mitochondrial unfolded protein response, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Mitochondria are the cell's power plants. When their proteins fold badly, the cell answers with a stress program that turns certain genes on.

A companion study had shown the response starts through a gene called chop and a partner called C/EBP beta. Here the team looked for the wider set of genes that follow, and for the promoter elements, the DNA switches that control them. Mapping that set helps explain how cells cope when their power plants are under strain.
plos-pone-0000974:
Kelly Rogers, Sandrine Picaud, Emilie Roncali and colleagues built a genetic way to watch calcium signals inside living mice, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Calcium surges inside cells help run many signaling pathways. Those surges are fast, local and hard to catch without cutting tissue.

Their approach makes cells produce a detectable signal when calcium rises, readable from outside the body. Non-invasive imaging means the same animal can be followed over time. It also lets signals be watched in deep tissues where microscopes cannot reach. Tools like this turn fleeting chemistry into a picture doctors and biologists can use.
plos-pone-0001074:
Guohua Yang, Peng Gao, Hua Zhang and colleagues found a kinesin mutation that worsens a root hair growth fault, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Root hairs grow only at their tips, making them a clean model for plant cell polarity. Plants with an always on form of the ROP2 switch lose that polarity and grow stunted, misshapen hairs.

A mutation in MRH2, a kinesin motor protein, enhanced that defect. Motors haul cargo along the cell's tracks, so a faulty motor deepening a polarity fault makes mechanical sense. The interaction maps two parts of the tip growth machine. Plant roots feed the world, and their smallest parts still hold basic lessons.
plos-pone-0001174:
The striatum is a set of deep brain structures involved in planning movements and in thinking. Javier Bernácer, Lucía Prensa, and José Manuel Giménez-Amaya mapped one of its cell types in the human brain. Their 2007 PLOS ONE article covers the cholinergic interneurons. These interneurons use the chemical acetylcholine and help coordinate the striatum's main output cells.

The authors describe how cholinergic interneurons are distributed differently across the caudate nucleus and putamen in humans. Detailed maps of the healthy human striatum are basic reference material. They matter for understanding diseases such as Parkinson's and Huntington's, where this region is central.
plos-pone-0001274:
Genome-wide association studies often include relatives, which complicates the statistics: related people share genes for reasons other than disease. Najaf Amin, Cornelia van Duijn, and Yurii Aulchenko present a method for that setting in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Genotyping hundreds of thousands of markers in thousands of subjects had created demand for fast, powerful, and reliable analysis methods.

Their genomic background based method performs association analysis in related individuals by accounting for the shared background. Family-based studies are common in isolated populations, where this problem is unavoidable. A sounder method protects such studies from false alarms.
plos-pone-0001374:
David Klinke wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on type 1 diabetes, a disease where the body can no longer make its own insulin. Doctors had long said that signs of the disease start when most insulin making cells are lost. The usual figure given was a loss of 80 to 95 percent. Klinke asked whether that loss alone can predict when illness starts.

He argues that the scale of cell loss matters, but it is not enough on its own to forecast onset. Other steps must shape the timing as well. The paper urges a broader view of how the disease builds. That view could shape how risk is judged in people near the start of illness.
plos-pone-0001474:
Paul Feldblum and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE trial report on a gel meant to block HIV in Nigeria. The gel, called SAVVY, was used in the vagina before sex. The trial enrolled women at high risk of HIV. It was a large phase 3 trial, with women split at random to gel or a dummy gel.

Women were followed for up to twelve months with regular HIV tests. The team weighed whether the gel cut new infections in real use. Gel based guards would give women a method they control themselves. Each such trial, win or lose, shapes the search for a workable guard.
plos-pone-0001574:
Tamar Geiger and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on odd traits when skin cells turn cancer like. As skin cancers grow, cells often shed their skin traits and gain a roving form. That shift is called EMT. The team tracked early stages of the shift in skin cells changed by a virus oncoprotein.

They found the shift here broke the usual pattern in key ways. Some marks moved in the wrong direction for classic EMT. Odd cases test the rules that cancer labs rely on. They show one road to cancer can bend the standard script, which matters for how early cancers are read.
plos-pone-0001674:
Shai Markman and co-authors reported that pollution changed both song and brain growth in a songbird, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Some pollutants disrupt hormones, and such disruption is known to cut breeding success in water animals. Far less was known about land animals living where land and water meet.

Exposed birds sang more complex songs, and the brain area called HVC, which controls song learning and production, was larger. The full text gives the exposure details, the song analysis, and the brain measurements. The result is a warning in an odd direction. A pollutant can make a mating signal stronger while still harming the animal. That could mislead both birds and the scientists who score their health by song.
plos-pone-0001774:
Peter Garvin, Lennart Nilsson, John Carstensen, and their co-authors measured a vessel-wall enzyme in healthy middle-aged people in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The enzyme is matrix metalloproteinase-9, or MMP-9, which cuts structural proteins in tissues. High circulating levels had been shown in patients with established coronary artery disease.

The team instead studied a population free of symptomatic heart disease and asked how MMP-9 levels associate with cardiovascular risk factors. The full text gives the blood values and the links to factors such as smoking and blood pressure. If MMP-9 tracks risk before symptoms start, it could join screening panels that aim to catch heart disease early.
plos-pone-0001874:
Ligia Antunes Goncalves and colleagues mapped a gene site that guards mice against malaria in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Genes were already known to help hosts resist the blood stage of the malaria parasite and to curb how sick they get. Far less was known about the liver stage, the first stop after the parasite enters the body.

The team used congenic mapping, breeding mouse lines that differ in one small stretch of DNA, to pin the effect to chromosome 17. They first showed that some mice carry fewer parasites in the liver. Finding the site is a step toward the gene itself, and toward why some hosts stop malaria early.
plos-pone-0001974:
Stephen Gammie and co-authors studied mouse mothers that neglect their pups, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Child neglect is the most common form of child maltreatment in humans, yet its biology is poorly known and no rodent model existed. The team had a mouse line, called MaD1, whose mothers by nature give pups little or no care.

They charted this line and asked what sets its mothers apart. As the title states, signaling by dopamine, a brain messenger tied to reward, was altered in these mice. If poor care has a brain basis that can be modeled, the model can be used to test what restores care.
plos-pone-0002074:
Scott Garforth, Michael Parniak, and Vinayaka Prasad tested whether HIV's copying enzyme can use a cheaper fuel, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. DNA polymerases, the enzymes that build DNA, normally use deoxynucleoside triphosphates, energy-rich building blocks. HIV reverse transcriptase is one such enzyme, and it is the target of many HIV drugs.

Cells also hold large amounts of diphosphate forms of the same blocks, with one less phosphate. The team asked whether HIV's enzyme can build DNA from those instead. If it can, drug tests that assume only the standard fuel may miss part of how the virus copies itself inside cells.
plos-pone-0002174:
Déborah Tribouillard-Tanvier, Suzana Dos Reis, Fabienne Gug, and co-authors tested how two anti-prion drugs work, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Prions are faulty proteins that cause fatal brain diseases. Two drugs with no structural likeness, 6AP and guanabenz, were found through a yeast test to block prions. Both also work against mammal prions in cells.

The team reports that the folding help given by ribosomal RNA is the shared target of both drugs. Ribosomal RNA helps assemble the cell's protein factories and can aid protein folding. A single shared target for two unlike drugs is a strong lead for designing better anti-prion treatments.
plos-pone-0002274:
James Hodge and Ralf Stanewsky studied a potassium channel inside the fruit fly's body clock, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The daily clock in the brain runs on molecular feedback loops, but the electrical activity of clock neurons matters too for rhythmic behavior. Most earlier work had distorted that activity with foreign channels or drugs, which makes results hard to read.

The authors focused on the fly's own Shaw potassium channel and its function within the clock network. Using the native channel gives a cleaner view of how electrical signaling keeps time. Work like this connects the clock's gene gears to the firing of real neurons.
plos-pone-0002374:
A research team led by Laaksonen reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Toni Laaksonen, Juan J. Negro, Sami Lyytinen, and others. Its subject is effects of Experimental Brood Size Manipulation and Gender on Carotenoid Levels of Eurasian Kestrels Falco tinnunculus. Animals use carotenoid-pigments for colouring, as antioxidants and as enhancers of the immune system.

Carotenoid-dependent colours can thus signal individual quality and carotenoids have also been suggested to mediate life-history trade-offs. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002474:
Work from Buchholz and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Kathrin Buchholz, Stefan Rahlfs, R. Heiner Schirmer, and others. Its subject is depletion of Plasmodium berghei Plasmoredoxin Reveals a Non-Essential Role for Life Cycle Progression of the Malaria Parasite. Proliferation of the pathogenic Plasmodium asexual blood stages in host erythrocytes requires an exquisite capacity to protect the malaria parasite against oxidative stress.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002574:
In 2008, He and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Xiao-Song He, Tyson H. Holmes, Sanae Sasaki, and others. Its subject is baseline Levels of Influenza-Specific CD4 Memory T-Cells Affect T-Cell Responses to Influenza Vaccines. Factors affecting immune responses to influenza vaccines have not been studied systematically.

We hypothesized that T-cell and antibody responses to the vaccines are functions of pre-existing host immunity against influenza antigens. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002674:
Naoya Yuhki led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was sequences, annotation and single nucleotide polymorphism of the major histocompatibility complex in the domestic cat. The catalog record names Naoya Yuhki first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Two sequences of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) regions in the domestic cat, 2.976 and 0.362 Mbps. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002774:
Gašper Tkačik led a team whose 2008 PLOS ONE article deals with the role of input noise in transcriptional regulation. Authorship is credited in the record to Gašper Tkačik and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Gene expression levels fluctuate even under constant external conditions. The summary also notes a further point. Much emphasis has usually been placed on the components of this noise that are due to randomness in transcription and translation. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002874:
Manoj Gambhir and Edwin Michael modeled lymphatic filariasis in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The disease is spread by vectors such as mosquitoes and is caused by a large parasitic worm. Global health programs were then weighing whether such diseases could be wiped out for good, not just held down.

Their model works through the complex ecology behind spread, including hosts, vectors, and worm life stages. It asks what those links mean for eradication, meaning full removal of transmission. Public health readers get a careful test of when control can become elimination and when the biology makes that goal much harder.
plos-pone-0002974:
Yi-Hong Wang and Michael Campbell reported odd flower changes after Agrobacterium transformation of tomato in 2008. Agrobacterium tumefaciens is the standard tool for adding genes to plants, and it is known to cause unexpected traits. Mutations in homeotic genes can also alter floral structure in known ways.

The transformed tomatoes showed unexpected flower phenotypes, yet their gene expression profiles stayed similar, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, that mismatch is the puzzle. Plant breeders using transformation need to know when a visible change reflects deep expression shifts and when it does not. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003074: Thomas Brody, Amarendra Yavatkar, Yong Lin and colleagues reported horizontal gene transfer links between a human MRSA pathogen and contagious bovine mastitis bacteria in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. MRSA is Staphylococcus aureus resistant to methicillin, and mastitis is an udder infection of cattle. The catalog record gives title, authors, and year, with no abstract detail beyond the title. The article presents evidence that gene exchange connects the human pathogen with bacteria behind a costly cattle disease.
plos-pone-0003174:
Hiroaki Kimura, Kin Ming Kwan, Zhaoping Zhang and colleagues identify a promoter of bone formation in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Bone mass is kept up by continuous remodeling, with repeated cycles of bone removal by osteoclasts and bone formation by osteoblasts. Many body-wide and local factors regulate that process. The team identified collagen triple helix repeat containing-1, called Cthrc1, in this context.

The title states that Cthrc1 is a positive regulator of osteoblastic bone formation. Readers learn of a factor that pushes the building side of bone turnover. Such factors interest researchers who seek new treatments for bone loss.
plos-pone-0003274: A. Roxana Lescano and colleagues published a case study in PLOS ONE in 2008 on research ethics training in Peru. The title states the full subject, and the work describes a training effort rather than a lab test. No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so this record adds no claims about outcomes or reach.
plos-pone-0007474: This 2009 paper introduces a laboratory tool for quickly rewriting proteins on demand. The system pairs a viral cutting enzyme with a rapamycin trigger, so adding the drug switches the cutter on and modifies target proteins fast. Researchers can use it to study what proteins do by changing them in real time inside living cells.
plos-pone-0007574: The protein Rho1 orchestrates how tissues take shape in developing animals. This study ran a genetic screen in fruit flies for other genes that modify Rho1's signal during wing-disc development. Each modifier found is a new suspect in the machinery that sculpts growing tissue.
plos-pone-0007674: Nerve cells fire using sodium channels built from segments S1 through S6. This study probed the shape and interactions of one piece, S2D4, in voltage-gated sodium channels. The structural details refine the model of how these molecular gates sense voltage and open.
plos-pone-0007774: A protein that binds selenium fades away in colon cancer, and this study asked why. The researchers found its gene is silenced by excessive methylation in tumors, and restoring it slowed cancer growth in cells and mice. SBP1 emerges as a lost guardian of the colon.
plos-pone-0007874: Breaking mitochondrial DNA replication in fruit flies paradoxically sped up mitochondrial transport along nerves. This study of pol γ disruption found faster axonal transport in vivo. The compensatory rush reveals how neurons cope with failing power plants.
plos-pone-0007974: High-end ultrasound is out of reach for most of the world. This paper proposes a new paradigm: 3D ultrasound powered by distributed networks, wireless links, and cloud computing. The vision could bring advanced imaging to the poorest clinics.
plos-pone-0008074: Food inspectors got a way to spot gene-modified ingredients without the standard DNA-copying test. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Zhou and colleagues fished GMO DNA out of samples with magnetic beads, then detected it with a light-based method. The usual test copies DNA billions of times, which can also copy contaminants and give false alarms. Skipping the copying step removes that risk. The direct detection held up in trials, offering a cleaner check for modified organisms in food.
plos-pone-0008174: Tuberculosis bacteria can lie dormant for decades, then wake. This study found small molecules that block the resuscitation-promoting factors that rouse them. The inhibitors could keep latent TB asleep — a new strategy against the world's deadliest bacterium.
plos-pone-0008274: Ovarian cancer was caught leaving marks in blood. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Teschendorff's team found a DNA-methylation signature in peripheral blood that flags active ovarian cancer. Blood-borne markers could catch the disease early. The team tested the signature's predictive power. The blood test prospect offers hope against a stealthy killer.
plos-pone-0008374: Mitochondrial ancestry got a rapid test. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Niederstatter and Parson built a light-based PCR assay for mtDNA haplogroup H screening. The cheap test also spots mixed samples well. Big population studies need such workhorses. The assay brings large mitochondrial surveys within reach of modest labs. Faster typing means more people screened.
plos-pone-0008474: Lupus kidney damage got a two-hit explanation. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Fenton's team showed anti-dsDNA antibodies start lupus nephritis while lost renal Dnase1 drives it.
